1	# Centered factorial effects and equivalent Gaussian parameterizations
2	
3	This offline packet contains the statistical definitions needed to interpret
4	the supplied calibration workflow. It is based on the version-matched PyMC
5	distribution documentation, the PyMC3 framework paper, and the Stan User's
6	Guide discussion of centered vectors.
7	
8	## 1. Factorial calibration model
9	
10	Suppose laboratories `l = 1, ..., L` measure the same response under protocols
11	`p = 1, ..., P`. A two-way Gaussian effects model can be written as
12	
13	$$
14	y_{lp} \sim
15	\mathcal{N}(\mu + a_l + b_p + g_{lp}, s_{lp}),
16	$$
17	
18	where `mu` is the grand mean, `a_l` is a laboratory effect, `b_p` is a
19	protocol effect, `g_lp` is a laboratory-by-protocol interaction, and `s_lp`
20	is the known standard error of the observed cell summary.
21	
22	Without identifying constraints, constants can be moved between the grand mean
23	and the main effects without changing fitted responses. A common convention is
24	
25	$$
26	\sum_{l=1}^{L} a_l = 0,
27	\qquad
28	\sum_{p=1}^{P} b_p = 0.
29	$$
30	
31	The interaction represents only the non-additive part of the response when it
32	is centered across both axes:
33	
34	$$
35	\sum_{l=1}^{L} g_{lp} = 0 \quad \text{for every } p,
36	\qquad
37	\sum_{p=1}^{P} g_{lp} = 0 \quad \text{for every } l.
38	$$
39	
40	These constraints define the interpretation of the effects. They are not
41	additional observations.
42	
43	## 2. Documented centered Gaussian distribution
44	
45	The source-version PyMC documentation describes `ZeroSumNormal` as a centered
46	Gaussian distribution for which one or more selected trailing axes sum to zero.
47	For one constrained axis of length `K`, the covariance is
48	
49	$$
50	\operatorname{Cov}(x) =
51	\sigma^2\left(I - \frac{1}{K}J\right),
52	$$
53	
54	where `I` is the identity matrix and every entry of `J` is one. The parameter
55	`sigma` is the standard deviation of the underlying unconstrained Normal used
56	by the construction. In this source version it is a positive scalar.
57	
58	By default the rightmost axis is constrained. The public API can constrain more
59	than one trailing axis. A matrix constrained over its last two axes therefore
60	has zero sums along both of those axes.
61	
62	## 3. Orthonormal reduced coordinates
63	
64	A zero-sum vector can be represented without redundancy. Let the columns of
65	`B` form an orthonormal basis for the subspace perpendicular to the all-ones
66	vector:
67	
68	$$
69	B^T B = I,
70	\qquad
71	B^T \mathbf{1} = 0.
72	$$
73	
74	If
75	
76	$$
77	z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I),
78	\qquad
79	x = Bz,
80	$$
81	
82	then `x` has the centered covariance above and lies on the zero-sum support.
83	Subtracting the mean from an unconstrained Gaussian vector is another way to
84	construct the same covariance.
85	
86	For a two-way interaction, bases for the laboratory and protocol centered
87	subspaces can be combined to represent exactly the matrices whose row and
88	column sums are zero.
89	
90	## 4. Reparameterization coherence
91	
92	A full constrained representation and an orthonormal reduced-coordinate
93	representation are two coordinate systems for the same statistical model. In a
94	linear-Gaussian analysis with the same priors, observations, and standard
95	errors, they must produce the same posterior fitted responses and the same
96	posterior summaries for any fixed linear contrast, up to numerical and Monte
97	Carlo error.
98	
99	This statement does not depend on a particular optimizer or sampler. Different
100	computational paths may represent the model differently internally, but they do
101	not define different prior shrinkage or different scientific contrasts.
102	
103	## 5. Planned interaction contrasts
104	
105	A difference-in-differences contrast compares a protocol change between two
106	laboratories. For laboratories `l_1`, `l_2` and protocols `p_1`, `p_2`,
107	one example is
108	
109	$$
110	C =
111	(\eta_{l_1 p_1} - \eta_{l_1 p_2})
112	-
113	(\eta_{l_2 p_1} - \eta_{l_2 p_2}),
114	$$
115	
116	where `eta_lp = mu + a_l + b_p + g_lp` is the fitted response. Additive grand,
117	laboratory, and protocol contributions cancel, so this contrast isolates a
118	laboratory-by-protocol interaction.
119	
120	Posterior means estimate the interaction contrast. Posterior standard
121	deviations and intervals quantify uncertainty. Both are properties of the
122	declared probability model.
123	
124	## 6. Sources
125	
126	- Salvatier, Wiecki, and Fonnesbeck, "Probabilistic programming in Python using
127	  PyMC3," *PeerJ Computer Science* 2:e55 (2016), DOI
128	  [10.7717/peerj-cs.55](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.55).
129	- PyMC documentation, `ZeroSumNormal` distribution API:
130	  [pymc.ZeroSumNormal](https://www.pymc.io/projects/docs/en/stable/api/distributions/generated/pymc.ZeroSumNormal.html).
131	- Stan User's Guide, "Parameterizing centered vectors":
132	  [centered-vector parameterization](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/regression.html#parameterizing-centered-vectors).
133	- Matching source-version documentation is retained in
134	  `source/pymc/distributions/multivariate.py`.
135	
136	These sources define the support, covariance, parameter meaning, model
137	identifiability, and equivalence needed for the investigation. They do not
138	prescribe a source-level repair.

"""End-to-end coherence checks (paper.md section 4):

1. NUTS sampling of a bare ZeroSumNormal prior (through ZeroSumTransform)
   must reproduce the documented covariance sigma^2 * tensor(P_axis).
2. The full centered factorial model from the public workflow must give the
   same posterior planned-contrast summaries as an orthonormal
   reduced-coordinate implementation of the same Gaussian model, up to Monte
   Carlo error.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

TASK_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(TASK_DIR / "source"))

import numpy as np

import pymc as pm


def basis(k: int) -> np.ndarray:
    m = np.eye(k) - np.ones((k, k)) / k
    u, _, _ = np.linalg.svd(m)
    return u[:, : k - 1]


def check_prior_mcmc(dims, sigma, draws=4000, tune=2000, seed=11):
    with pm.Model():
        pm.ZeroSumNormal("x", sigma=sigma, shape=dims, n_zerosum_axes=len(dims))
        idata = pm.sample(
            draws=draws, tune=tune, chains=2, cores=1, random_seed=seed,
            progressbar=False, compute_convergence_checks=False,
        )
    xs = idata.posterior["x"].values.reshape(-1, *dims)
    ref = np.eye(1) * sigma**2
    for k in dims:
        ref = np.kron(ref, np.eye(k) - np.ones((k, k)) / k)
    emp = np.cov(xs.reshape(len(xs), -1).T)
    err = float(np.max(np.abs(emp - ref))) / sigma**2
    scale = 2.0 / np.sqrt(len(xs))  # rough MC tolerance for cov entries
    tag = "OK " if err < 3 * scale else "??"
    print(f"[{tag}] prior MCMC dims={dims} sigma={sigma}: max scaled cov diff {err:.3e} (mc~{scale:.1e})")
    return err


def main():
    print("== prior NUTS-through-transform covariance ==")
    check_prior_mcmc((4,), 0.7)
    check_prior_mcmc((3, 4), 0.6)

    case = json.loads((TASK_DIR / "fixtures" / "factorial_calibration_study.json").read_text())
    labs = case["laboratories"]
    prots = case["protocols"]
    y = np.asarray(case["cell_estimates"], float)
    s = np.asarray(case["cell_standard_errors"], float)
    sc = case["prior_scales"]
    L, P = len(labs), len(prots)

    common = dict(draws=4000, tune=2000, chains=2, cores=1, random_seed=777,
                  progressbar=False, compute_convergence_checks=False)

    with pm.Model():
        mu = pm.Normal("mu", 0.0, sc["grand_mean"])
        a = pm.ZeroSumNormal("a", sigma=sc["laboratory"], shape=L)
        b = pm.ZeroSumNormal("b", sigma=sc["protocol"], shape=P)
        g = pm.ZeroSumNormal("g", sigma=sc["interaction"], shape=(L, P), n_zerosum_axes=2)
        eta = mu + a[:, None] + b[None, :] + g
        pm.Normal("y", mu=eta, sigma=s, observed=y)
        ida = pm.sample(**common)

    with pm.Model():
        mu = pm.Normal("mu", 0.0, sc["grand_mean"])
        za = pm.Normal("za", 0.0, sc["laboratory"], shape=L - 1)
        zb = pm.Normal("zb", 0.0, sc["protocol"], shape=P - 1)
        zg = pm.Normal("zg", 0.0, sc["interaction"], shape=(L - 1) * (P - 1))
        bl, bp = basis(L), basis(P)
        a = bl @ za
        b = bp @ zb
        g = (np.kron(bl, bp) @ zg).reshape(L, P)
        eta = mu + a[:, None] + b[None, :] + g
        pm.Normal("y", mu=eta, sigma=s, observed=y)
        pm.Deterministic("a", a)
        pm.Deterministic("b", b)
        pm.Deterministic("g", g)
        idb = pm.sample(**common)

    pa, pb = ida.posterior, idb.posterior
    eta_a = (pa["mu"] + pa["a"] + pa["b"] + pa["g"]).values  # broadcast
    eta_b = (pb["mu"] + pb["a"] + pb["b"] + pb["g"]).values

    print("\n== posterior fitted-cell comparison (mean/sd across cells) ==")
    for name, (xa, xb) in {
        "grand_mean": (pa["mu"].values.ravel(), pb["mu"].values.ravel()),
        "a": (pa["a"].values.reshape(-1, L), pb["a"].values.reshape(-1, L)),
        "b": (pa["b"].values.reshape(-1, P), pb["b"].values.reshape(-1, P)),
        "g": (pa["g"].values.reshape(-1, L, P), pb["g"].values.reshape(-1, L, P)),
        "eta": (eta_a.reshape(-1, L, P), eta_b.reshape(-1, L, P)),
    }.items():
        dm = float(np.max(np.abs(xa.mean(0) - xb.mean(0))))
        ds = float(np.max(np.abs(xa.std(0) - xb.std(0))))
        print(f"  {name:10s} max|dmean|={dm:.4f} max|dsd|={ds:.4f}")

    print("\n== planned contrasts ==")
    ea = eta_a.reshape(-1, L, P)
    eb = eta_b.reshape(-1, L, P)
    lab_i = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(labs)}
    prt_i = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(prots)}
    worst_m = worst_s = 0.0
    for c in case["planned_contrasts"]:
        va = np.zeros(len(ea))
        vb = np.zeros(len(eb))
        for t in c["terms"]:
            va += t["coefficient"] * ea[:, lab_i[t["laboratory"]], prt_i[t["protocol"]]]
            vb += t["coefficient"] * eb[:, lab_i[t["laboratory"]], prt_i[t["protocol"]]]
        dm = abs(va.mean() - vb.mean())
        ds = abs(va.std(ddof=1) - vb.std(ddof=1))
        q_a = np.quantile(va, [0.05, 0.95]); q_b = np.quantile(vb, [0.05, 0.95])
        dq = float(np.max(np.abs(q_a - q_b)))
        worst_m = max(worst_m, dm); worst_s = max(worst_s, ds)
        print(f"  {c['name']:32s} centered mean={va.mean():+.4f} sd={va.std(ddof=1):.4f} | reduced mean={vb.mean():+.4f} sd={vb.std(ddof=1):.4f} | dmean={dm:.4f} dsd={ds:.4f} dq90={dq:.4f}")
    print(f"\nworst contrast dmean={worst_m:.4f} dsd={worst_s:.4f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

## Root cause

The defect is in `ZeroSumNormal.logp` (`source/pymc/distributions/multivariate.py:2780`). The documented model (paper.md §2–4) is a Gaussian on the zero-sum support with covariance σ²(I − J/K) per constrained axis — equivalently `x = Bz` with `z ~ N(0, σ²I)` against orthonormal reduced coordinates, whose density is −d/2·log(2πσ²) − ‖x‖²/2σ² with d = ∏(Kᵢ−1).

The implementation instead computed `pm.logp(normal_dist, value) × d/n` (n = full support size). That factor shrinks the quadratic form by d/n — effectively an inflated prior variance with a mismatched normalizer — while `random()` drew from the *correct* documented covariance. So sampling completed and all sum-to-zero constraints held, yet the implemented prior (hence posterior shrinkage and every planned contrast) silently differed from the documented Gaussian model. A second latent flaw computed the degrees of freedom from `value.shape[-k:]`, which produces wrong values as soon as the value carries batch dimensions.

```python

    + _removed_constraints * 0.5 * pt.log(2 * np.pi * sigma**2)
```
